I am 58 years old, and I have worked this land in Quzhou County for 40 years. My 10.1 mu farm is all I have, and at this age, I do not take risks. My household has only two people—my husband and me—because our children work in the city and only come back during harvest if they can get leave. This means every decision I make must account for our limited backs and limited time.

It is now late April. The winter wheat I sowed last October is at the jointing stage. I will go out tomorrow to spread urea as a topdressing—about 10 kg per mu on top of the basal fertilizer I applied before sowing. I irrigate using my well. I will water the wheat once now at jointing, and once more at grain filling if the sky gives us no rain. Three irrigations in total for the wheat season is enough; more wastes electricity and water. For pests, I watch carefully. If I see aphids or signs of powdery mildew, I spray. I expect two sprayings will be necessary this spring. I planted an improved wheat variety that has done well on this land for years. I know what to expect from it.

After we harvest the wheat in early June—usually around June 10—we have a narrow window. I will hire a combine harvester to cut the wheat, and then I will use a no-tillage seeder to plant hybrid maize directly into the wheat stubble. Some neighbors still rotary till, but at my age I cannot afford the extra labor and the tight turnaround. The hybrid maize seed costs more, but the yield is worth it. I will apply compound fertilizer at sowing, then topdress with urea at the big-flare stage. Maize needs water at jointing and grain filling, so I will irrigate twice. I also watch for corn borer and armyworm—two pesticide applications should handle them.

My education helps me read the county agricultural bureau's notices, but experience teaches me that chasing maximum yield with extra fertilizer is foolish. The soil here is already fertile from decades of farming. I keep my nitrogen at moderate levels—around 15–16 kg per mu total for each crop—because over-fertilizing wastes money and makes the plants lodge. My goal is not to win a yield contest; it is to get a reliable harvest of about 500 kg per mu for wheat and 550 kg per mu for maize, which covers our household grain needs and leaves some to sell.
